avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred

Routine transthoracic / bubble echocardiogram (PFO screening) is NOT indicated in migraine with aura; PFO-migraine association is controversial and PFO closure does not reduce migraine [Charles_2017]

key_clinical_evidence: Migralepsy (ICHD-3 1.4.4) is a seizure triggered by migraine aura — requires aura to be temporally followed by a seizure
Reversible MRI signal changes are recognised in hemiplegic migraine and should not be misinterpreted as permanent infarct
Hemiplegic migraine workup must exclude MELAS, autoimmune encephalitis, and structural causes
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: ICHD-3: the diagnosis is made on the structured history. Imaging is for the red flags that history screens for, not for the diagnosis.
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: No laboratory test contributes to a migraine diagnosis; a targeted assay belongs to a specific suspicion.

July 2026 review applied end to end: ICHD-3 history/examination is required in all cases; routine MRI, EEG, ECG, CSF, echocardiography, cardiac monitoring and laboratory panels are absent. Retained tests answer an explicit atypical-aura, seizure, infarct, MELAS, CADASIL or aneurysm question.

mri.impression: 1. Diffuse left hemispheric cortical swelling with T2/FLAIR gyral cortical hyperintensity and mild sulcal effacement. 2. Critically, DWI is NORMAL — no restricted diffusion, no cytotoxic oedema. No leptomeningeal or cortical enhancement. 3. Normal MRA — no arterial occlusion, stenosis, or dissection. The pattern of vasogenic cortical oedema without cytotoxic oedema and non-territorial distribution does not conform to an arterial infarct. Imaging differential includes cortical spreading depression, autoimmune encephalitis, and other causes of cortical vasogenic oedema. Follow-up MRI is recommended to assess reversibility

patient.history_present_illness: A 26-year-old woman presented to the emergency department brought by her partner with a 3-hour history of severe left-sided throbbing headache that began approximately 30 minutes after she developed blurred vision in her right visual field. Shortly after the headache peaked, her partner noticed that she was struggling to find words and her right arm appeared weak. Within the following hour she experienced two brief episodes of right-hand rhythmic jerking lasting approximately 90 seconds each, during which she was unresponsive, followed by postictal confusion lasting approximately 20 minutes. She has had episodes of unilateral throbbing headache accompanied by transient arm weakness affecting alternating sides since the age of 14. During those earlier attacks, the weakness has always resolved completely within a few hours, and previous assessments including head CT, brain MRI, MR angiography, lumbar puncture, and basic metabolic and mitochondrial blood tests were all documented as normal at age 17 and again at age 22. She was commenced on topiramate 75 mg twice daily approximately two years ago following inadequate response to flunarizine; despite this she continues to have one to two attacks monthly. There is no family history of similar episodes, hemiplegic migraine, or any neurological condition. She does not smoke, drinks alcohol only occasionally, and uses no illicit substances. She takes topiramate and a combined oral contraceptive pill (Mercilon, desogestrel 150 mcg / ethinylestradiol 20 mcg). She has no known drug allergies.
